title: Confined workers cannot use ordinary relocation
statement: While confinement continues, the compound's workers have no access to public relocation or its transport. Their only protection is backup cooling inside the compound. In the main case, confinement continues through the heat episode. A comparison opens access at hour 4. After that, unprotected workers share the remaining formal places and transport with town residents in proportion to their numbers, with no added capacity.
rationale: Reports on these compounds describe confiscated passports, guarded perimeters and punishment when workers ask for help. This removes the ordinary routes to outside assistance. Confinement changes access and exposure, not the physiological rate. Workers face the same transferred heat risk as town residents, unless the transfer factors are set to different values. The comparison with early access is an analytical test, not an estimated time of rescue.
evidence_needed: Movement of confined workers during a power or heat emergency at such a compound.

decided.by: Machine red-team author; identity and independent approval not verified

elicitation.question: Would confined workers be released or evacuated once the power failed during a heatwave?
elicitation.argument: The operator holds the workers against their will and has its own reasons to keep them inside; losing power does not unlock the compound, and emergency services have no standing access to it.
elicitation.dissent: A prolonged emergency could break down control of the compound, or the operator or authorities could move workers, reducing exposure well below the modeled level.
elicitation.falsifier: A documented compound emergency in which confined workers left or were moved at material scale.

title: Chosen costs and clinical ranges of a blackout in a heat wave, at 2025 prices
statement: SC41 chooses the extra cost of cooled places and of private moves, 25 US dollars a person-day (from 0 to 100), and the extra cost of medical care, 15,000 US dollars for each serious casualty (from 0 to 50,000), at 2025 prices. It takes the heatstroke share of heat emergency visits, the share of those visits that ends in death and the share admitted to hospital from national studies, and chooses a range around each value. Economic loss adds customers' interruption costs, the restoration work and these extra costs. It counts no lost value added.
rationale: No source gives these costs for an outage in a heat wave, so the scenario chooses them. National studies of emergency visits give the clinical shares; the ranges are chosen to cover other settings. Outages add hospital admissions and put hospitals under strain, which the extra cost of care stands for. Each person is counted once among the serious casualties.
evidence_needed: Local costs of cooled places, private moves and heat care during an outage. Local shares of heatstroke visits, of the visits that end in death and of the admissions.

title: Highest equivalent outdoor temperature for heat-related deaths
statement: The equivalent outdoor temperature that drives heat-related deaths is capped at 55 °C by default, as the method's authors do for the heat-related mortality estimates in Phoenix; the cap is an input from 55 °C to 230 °C. The all-cause mortality curve and the emergency-visit curve are not capped, as in the method.
rationale: The 2026 paper constrains equivalent temperatures to 55 °C only for its heat-related mortality estimates in Phoenix, because those risk ratios are already very high in the observed range. It states no such limit for all-cause mortality, whose Phoenix risk ratios reach 6.38. An earlier reading applied the cap to every curve, which held the risk of a home in full darkness at the risk of a home at about 30 °C.
evidence_needed: An observed relation between indoor heat during outages and deaths, to test the equivalent-temperature conversion beyond the fitted range.

supports.note: The authors replace equivalent temperatures above 55 °C with 55 °C for the heat-related mortality estimates in Phoenix only.

title: Time to check protection before switching back on
statement: Switching back on waits for checks of the protection settings, which finish 24 hours after the cyber cause is determined by default; the range is 6 to 72 hours.
rationale: No source gives how long such checks take. In a no-notice cyber event the first 12-24 hours go to standing up response teams, and switching tampered equipment back on can damage it and endanger crews, so the checks come first. Ukraine 2015 restored service by hand within six hours, which sets the low end; the 72-hour high end is chosen.
evidence_needed: Measured durations of protection-setting verification after cyber incidents on distribution control systems.

supports.note: The first 12-24 hours of a no-notice cyber event go to standing up response teams and assessing impacts.
Switching back on after a cyber breach can endanger crews and damage equipment.
Ukraine 2015: service restored by hand switching within six hours.
The 2016 relay attack aimed to make quick manual reclosing damaging, the risk that checks guard against.

title: Share of heatstroke as severe as intensive-care cases
statement: 10% of the people seriously ill with heatstroke are as severe as the Chicago 1995 intensive-care patients, and 28% of those die within a year of the event. The share ranges from 2% to 30%.
rationale: Dematte et al. followed 58 intensive-care heatstroke patients: 21% died in hospital and a further 28% within a year. About 55% of heatstroke emergency visits are admitted, but no source gives the intensive-care share, so 10% is chosen within a wide range.
evidence_needed: The share of heatstroke patients needing intensive care, and one-year mortality after heatstroke of all severities.

supports.note: A further 28% of 58 intensive-care heatstroke patients died within one year.

title: Rework from the AI's changes
statement: The attacker keeps a hidden route to the protection settings until it stops. When the crews start to switch circuits back on, an attacker that still has the route changes the settings again on the circuits not yet back, 15 minutes later for an AI and 48 hours later for a human team. Crews then stop switching until the attacker has stopped, and redo one third of the switching work still to do before they go on. The attacker's timed job runs once, 60 hours after the outage, unless it is cancelled first or every circuit is back; it adds one third of the switching work still to do. The share ranges from 0 to 1.
rationale: Re-energising after a cyber breach should not be attempted unless the grid can be verified safe, and changed protection can turn a restart into damage, so crews do not switch while the settings keep changing under them. Each change the actor makes adds work and never undoes circuits that are back, as the decision memo requires. The one-third share, the job's time and the actor's pace are chosen for this scenario; the pace follows the catalogue's tempo assumption.
evidence_needed: Records of how much restoration work an adversary's repeated changes to protection settings added in a real incident.

supports.note: Switching after a cyber breach should wait until the grid can be verified safe.
The 2016 relay attack aimed at changed protection when operators switched back.
An adversary kept access to an operational network for months.

title: People on home devices: backup, outreach and admission
statement: Home device batteries last 3 hours (range 2 to 12 hours). A quarter of device users have an alternative power supply that runs their device through the outage. When outreach starts, at the hour the cooled places open in each response, responders move half of the device users who are without power and not seriously ill to sites with power. After their backup runs out, people on a home ventilator who are still without power are admitted to hospital at 0.02 per hour and people on an oxygen concentrator at a quarter of that rate. Concentrators are 99% of the device mix.
rationale: In Sapporo in 2018, 83 of 230 home-ventilator users were admitted (36%). Taking about 8 hours of battery and about 30 hours of outage (a chosen value; the source gives no Sapporo duration), -ln(1 - 0.36) / 22 is about 0.02 per hour. Concentrator users depend less acutely on power; the quarter is chosen. New York 2003 device-failure admissions rose many-fold within days, which agrees with admissions early in an outage. The outreach share is chosen; responders can find device users from the emPOWER lists.
evidence_needed: Admissions of home oxygen-concentrator users by outage duration.

supports.note: 83 of 230 home-ventilator users admitted during the 2018 blackout (abstract).
Concentrators are about 99% of the electricity-dependent device mix.
Concentrator batteries last about 2 to 4 hours, up to 12 with external packs.
Device-failure hospitalisations rose sharply in the 2003 New York outage.

title: Share of cooled places with their own power
statement: By default no cooled place has its own backup power, so none opens during the blackout; an option gives every place power. The range is 0 to 100%.
rationale: Stone et al. 2021 found that none of the three cities' cooling-centre plans required backup power, and during Hurricane Beryl Houston's designated cooling sites could not be used without power.

title: Cost of an hour of restoration work
statement: One lineworker-hour of restoration work costs $91.66 in 2025 dollars: the 2025 median wage of power-line installers, $45.83 an hour, times 2 for benefits, overtime, vehicles and equipment. The standard crews are 40 lineworkers. The multiplier ranges from 1.5 to 4 and the crews from 10 to 200 lineworkers.
rationale: Utilities book storm restoration as incremental labour, contractor and material costs, as Florida's rule applied to FPL's Hurricane Ian costs shows. No source gives the loaded cost of a switching hour after a cyber event, so the multiplier is chosen.
evidence_needed: Utility filings of incremental restoration cost per crew-hour, and the crews a utility of this size sends to a supply-wide outage.

supports.note: Median 2025 wage of electrical power-line installers and repairers, $45.83 an hour.

title: All-cause mortality curve
statement: The all-cause mortality curve is the Gasparrini et al. 2015 curve for the setting by default: weight 1 for it and 0 for the other three studies that the method's authors list (Bobb et al. 2014, Nordio et al. 2015, Schwartz et al. 2016). The weights are inputs.
rationale: The 2026 paper pools the four studies with weights from the inverse variance of each slope, but the variances are not published. Its Phoenix all-cause risk ratios reach 6.38 with the grid operating. Under equal weights the pooled curve reaches 6.38 only at an equivalent temperature of about 150 °C; the Gasparrini curve reaches it at about 71 °C, so the authors' weights must give the Gasparrini curve most of the weight. The other three curves are straight lines fitted over the whole warm season, while the Gasparrini curve is fitted to the shape of the hot end. Stone et al. 2023 used the Gasparrini curve alone for the blackout.
evidence_needed: The standard errors of each study's slope for the setting, to rebuild the authors' weights.

supports.note: The four Phoenix all-cause curves.
Phoenix all-cause risk ratios reach 6.38 with the grid operating.
The authors pool the studies by inverse-variance weights from an unpublished file.

title: The people on the supply
statement: One supply serves 60,000 people (range 20,000 to 120,000). 10,000 of them (range 0 to 20,000) are held in a compound whose gates its operators control. Every group follows the national age mix: 82.3% under 65, 10.4% aged 65 to 74 and 7.3% aged 75 and over. Among the people outside the compound, 0.242% of those under 65 and 2.185% of those 65 and over live on a home oxygen concentrator or ventilator. Each band's normal death rate is the national rate for 2023: 0.00276, 0.0180 and 0.0670 deaths per person-year.
rationale: The setting names no city. The age mix and death rates are national, so they fit a setting of any size; the device shares are the published prevalence for the West census region and for people 65 and over. The compound and its size follow the scenario's story.
evidence_needed: Local counts by age, device use and confinement for a real setting.

supports.note: The age shares.

title: The heat wave
statement: A heat wave starts with the outage and lasts 120 hours (range 48 to 240 hours). Its daily mean outdoor temperature is 39.35 °C (range 30 to 45 °C), the mean of the five daily means of the July 2006 Phoenix heat wave. The outage adds heat risk only while the heat wave lasts.
rationale: The five-day event is the one the method's authors simulate, and its weather is the default for a hot, dry setting. After the heat wave the scenario assumes that homes without power are no longer dangerous; the curves of the method describe heat-wave temperatures. Humidity is not an input, because higher humidity at the same temperature is not associated with higher mortality.
evidence_needed: Indoor temperatures and deaths in homes without power after a heat wave ends.

supports.note: The five daily means; 39.35 °C is their mean (arithmetic).
The source's blackout scenario lasts the same five days.
Humidity at the same temperature slightly lowers mortality.

title: Heat risk from experienced temperature
statement: Without power, a group's experienced temperature rises from 26.3 °C toward 35.7 °C with a heat-up time of 12 hours (range 6 to 48 hours), and returns to 26.3 °C as soon as power returns. The equivalent outdoor temperature is the outdoor temperature plus the rise divided by the group's slope, 0.208 °C per °C (range 0.1 to 0.4). In each age band the outage adds deaths at the larger of two excess rates: the band's normal death rate times the rise in the all-cause risk ratio, and the normal rate of heat-related deaths, 0.07 a day in 1.39 million people, times the rise in the heat-related risk ratio at the capped equivalent temperature. Heat emergency visits follow the Phoenix heat-related curve from a normal rate of 5.9 visits a day in 1.39 million people. Each person counts at most one visit: the visits that a person at home would have so far set the chance of a first visit. 5.4% of first visits are heatstroke, and each counts as one person.
rationale: This is the experienced-temperature method of Stone et al. 2023 and Gronlund et al. 2026, with one slope for each group. Heat-related deaths are part of all deaths, so the excess of all deaths is at least the larger of the two published estimates; in the 2026 paper the heat-related estimate for Phoenix is eleven times the all-cause estimate. The temperature in full darkness comes from the source's mean over its outage profile. People with power, with backup, in a cooled place or moved away keep the temperature with power, so the outage adds no risk for them. The method sums each person's risk over the heat wave and limits it to one. At the lowest slopes the curve otherwise gives each person at home more than one visit an hour, and heatstroke reaches most of them. The model applies the limit in the same form as deaths: the expected visits so far set the chance that a person has had a first visit.
evidence_needed: Observed deaths among people without cooling in homes whose temperature was measured during an outage. Counts of heatstroke among people without cooling at very high indoor temperatures, to test the limit of one visit for each person and the heatstroke share at that heat.

supports.note: The analog-temperature method, and its limit of one on each person's summed risk.

title: Backup, private moves and cooled places
statement: A tenth of the people in homes and a tenth of the compound's people have backup cooling that works through the heat wave; a quarter in a comparison. A tenth of the other people in homes move away privately between hours 4 and 28. Cooled places hold 2% of the people on the supply at one time, and a place opens only if it has its own power. Officials open the places at hour 4, 18 or 36 and move 2,000, 800 or 150 people an hour in the early, standard and delayed responses, up to 2,000 an hour. Only people not yet seriously ill are admitted, in proportion to the people who wait. The compound's people can use places only if officials open its gates.
rationale: The authors of the method judge that cooling centres hold no more than 1 to 2% of a city's people in a concurrent heat wave and blackout, and that no plan required backup power. The backup, private-move and response values are chosen for this scenario, as in the earlier blackout case.
evidence_needed: Local counts of homes with working backup cooling, private relocation in outages, and the opening and intake of powered cooling centres.

supports.note: No more than 1 to 2% of the population; no backup power required.

title: Customers' costs of the interruption
statement: The supply serves 24,000 residential and 3,000 non-residential customers. A customer's cost is its 24-hour cost from the ICE 2 calculator, $56.66 for a residential and $13,878 for a non-residential customer, times the outage hours divided by 24 to a power fitted through the 2-hour and 24-hour values: 0.663 and 0.546. Beyond 24 hours the same power continues.
rationale: The fit passes through the calculator's 2-hour and 24-hour values and is within 3% of its 8-hour values. The calculator's surveys were not designed for interruptions longer than 24 hours, so the longer part is a convention. The customer counts are chosen for a supply of 60,000 people.
evidence_needed: Customer counts for the utility, and surveyed costs of interruptions longer than a day.

supports.note: The 2-, 8- and 24-hour costs by customer class.
The surveys were not designed for interruptions over 24 hours.

title: Switching the circuits back on
statement: With intact equipment and no checks, the standard crews switch every circuit of the supply back on in 15 hours (range 6 to 30 hours). Circuits come back one by one as the work is done, and a circuit that is back stays back. Switching starts when the AI's known remote route is cut, the cyber cause is determined and the checks of the protection settings are complete. Switching stops while an attacker that keeps its route changes the settings again, and resumes once the attacker has stopped.
rationale: After blackouts with intact plant, service came back in about 6 to 30 hours: within six hours by hand in Ukraine in 2015, in 6 to 12 hours in the Pacific Southwest in 2011, in 12 to 16 hours in Iberia in 2025 and in about 30 hours in New York in 2003. Utilities restore a circuit in sections and add segments as the pickup load settles. The 15-hour default is chosen within that span.
evidence_needed: A restoration curve for manual switching after a cyber event on a distribution utility.

supports.note: Ukrainian utilities restored power by hand within six hours in 2015.
